basic_info.name: Matchbox (matchbox.health)
basic_info.description: Matchbox is an open-source FHIR validation and mapping server from the Swiss vendor ahdis ag, built as a fork of the hapifhir/hapi-fhir-jpaserver-starter and wrapping the same official HL7 Java reference validator (org.hl7.fhir.core) that HAPI uses, plus a FHIR Mapping Language engine. Its load-bearing fact for MediKiosk is that it is designed specifically for offline and production profile validation: implementation guides can be preloaded from classpath, filesystem or an absolute package URL, an internal terminology server can replace tx.fhir.org, and it can run as a Docker microservice or as a Java library (matchbox-engine) with no internet call-outs. It exposes $validate (with auto-installation of an IG package when httpReadOnly is disabled), $install-npm-package, StructureMap/$transform, Questionnaire/$extract (SDC) and CDA-to-FHIR mapping, and has shipped extremely frequently through 2026 - current release v4.1.16 (2026-09-14), tracking HAPI FHIR 8.12.0 and org.hl7.fhir.core 6.10.4. It is used at IHE Connectathons (integrated into the Gazelle EVS Client) and in the Swiss e-health community. The NDHM/ABDM NRCeS package (ndhm.in) is not preloaded or documented for Matchbox, but the generic NPM-package loading mechanism it uses (registry, direct package.tgz, classpath or file system) is the same one that would load ndhm.in, so ABDM profile validation appears technically supported though publicly unverified. It is JVM infrastructure (JDK 17+, recommended >=2.5 GB RAM, and a 12 GB Docker heap default since v4.1.3) and therefore belongs off-device as a build-time or clinic-side validator, not on a 4 GB kiosk.
basic_info.organization: ahdis ag (Zürich, Switzerland), a health-interoperability consultancy led by Oliver Egger (oliveregger), which also sells commercial support. Built on the HAPI FHIR project and the official HL7 FHIR validator/mapping-language implementation, both open source.
basic_info.country: Switzerland (ahdis ag, Zürich). Primary market is Swiss e-health (CH EPR/FHIR) and IHE Connectathons internationally; not an India-specific project.
basic_info.status: Production and very actively maintained. Latest tagged release v4.1.16 shipped 2026-09-14, two days before verification, with v4.1.15 on 2026-09-11; the whole 4.1.x line has released roughly every few days-to-weeks through 2026. GitHub at verification: 37 stars, 29 forks, 5 watchers, 2,001 commits, 9 open issues, 1 open pull request. Public development and test servers run at test.ahdis.ch/matchbox/fhir and test.ahdis.ch/matchboxv3/fhir.

technical_features.what_it_does: Matchbox validates FHIR resources and Bundles against base FHIR R4/R4B/R5 and against any loaded Implementation Guide profiles, and transforms health data using the FHIR Mapping Language. It exposes the standard FHIR $validate operation (system- and instance-level), where the caller supplies the resource plus a profile canonical and optionally an ig parameter (e.g. ig=ch-core#3.0.0); the response is an OperationOutcome with errors, warnings and hints, enriched with the loaded-package list, validator parameters and duration. It also exposes $install-npm-package to load an IG at runtime, StructureMap/$transform for mapping, Questionnaire/$extract for SDC, and a /validate + /profiles API that IHE's Gazelle EVS Client consumes at Connectathons. For Module C the function that matters is: take an emitted OPConsultRecord/DocumentBundle, point Matchbox at the NRCeS ndhm.in IG (if loaded), and get a deterministic pass/fail OperationOutcome offline.
technical_features.architecture: Maven reactor with two main modules: matchbox-engine (the standalone Java library, derived from org.hl7.fhir.core's validator and mapping-language implementation, with a few CDA/package-handling classes patched in) and matchbox-server (a Spring Boot microservice built on the hapi-fhir-jpaserver-starter, adding the FHIR API, Gazelle API, internal terminology server, validation statistics and an Angular GUI with in-browser resource validation). A matchbox-engine-cli fat jar (>100 MB) is also published. It maintains cached validation engines per Implementation Guide and version; onlyOneEngine mode (development) allows creating/updating conformance resources with a single engine. IG loading sources are, in order: FHIR package servers, absolute http URL to a package, classpath, or local filesystem. The official HL7 Java validator version is pinned per Matchbox release.
technical_features.inputs: FHIR resources or Bundles as application/fhir+json or application/fhir+xml; the target profile canonical and optionally an explicit ig#version; loaded NPM IG packages (embedded or fetched); StructureMap/FML maps and source data for transforms; an optional external terminology server URL or Matchbox's internal one. It is content-agnostic - it does not ingest dialogue, audio or documents, only already-structured FHIR.
technical_features.outputs: An OperationOutcome (errors/warnings/information with expression paths, plus loaded packages and validator parameters); transformed FHIR/CDA resources from StructureMap/$transform and CDA-to-FHIR maps; a list of validatable profiles via Bundle/$get-profiles or the Gazelle /profiles API; validation statistics. For Module C the relevant output is a machine-checkable OperationOutcome for an emitted ABDM bundle - not a clinical summary.
technical_features.standards_compliance: Conformance is real and machine-checked rather than claimed: Matchbox validates against FHIR R4 (4.0.1), R4B and R5 using the official HL7 Java reference validator, so any loaded IG's mandatory fields, cardinalities, invariants and bindings are enforced. It ships IPS and Swiss IG support out of the box and is used to validate IHE profiles (MHD, PDQm, PCF). ABDM/NRCeS conformance is a property of loading the ndhm.in package, not of Matchbox itself: the current published NRCeS IG is ndhm.in v6.5.0 (2025-05-08, FHIR R4) and it is distributed as an NPM package on registry.fhir.org/packages.simplifier.net and as package.tgz at nrces.in. Matchbox's documented loading paths (package server, absolute http URL, classpath, filesystem) can all carry ndhm.in, and $validate auto-installs a package when httpReadOnly is disabled - however, no public Matchbox deployment, configuration example or issue that explicitly loads ndhm.in was found, and Matchbox's own test servers preload Swiss IGs, so ABDM-profile validation through Matchbox is technically plausible but publicly unverified. [uncertain] Terminology checking of SNOMED CT/LOINC requires the external terminology server or expanded resources; Matchbox's internal terminology server deliberately does not validate display names and cannot expand intensional ValueSets, so those code checks are skipped offline unless a full tx server is provided.
technical_features.offline_capability: Offline is a first-class, documented strength and the main reason to prefer Matchbox over a bare validator: Matchbox Engine exists explicitly to allow standalone validation 'without the need for a connection to the internet', IG packages can be loaded directly from the classpath or filesystem, the terminology server can be pointed at Matchbox's own internal endpoint, and a Docker image can be pre-baked with packages at build time via --hapi.fhir.only_install_packages=true so startup needs no internet. In httpReadOnly deployment mode, IGs can only be loaded through configuration, which is the safe posture for a locked-down clinic/kiosk-side validator. This aligns cleanly with MediKiosk's offline-first and India-residency constraints; the only care points are pre-vendoring the ndhm.in package, and the fact that terminology completeness offline depends on the internal tx server's limits.
technical_features.languages_supported: Not a natural-language tool. FHIR strings (CodeableConcept.text, Narrative, translation extensions) can carry Hindi/Devanagari or Hinglish content, but Matchbox performs no tokenisation, transliteration or bilingual rendering. [uncertain] No AYUSH or Indic-script-specific behaviour was found.
technical_features.deployment_model: Runs as (a) a Spring Boot/Docker microservice in a clinic/LAN/room server or CI host, (b) a standalone Java library embedded in an application (matchbox-engine, Maven health.matchbox:matchbox-engine), or (c) a CLI fat jar. Requires a JVM; the engine requires JDK 11+ (JRE 17 support re-added in v4.1.6), and the server has tracked JDK 17/21 (v3.8.1 upgraded to JDK 21 LTS). A PostgreSQL database is used for persistent IG storage (H2/config without preloaded IGs otherwise). Resource guidance: docs recommend at least 2.5 GB RAM for the container depending on IGs installed, and v4.1.3 raised the Docker heap requirement to 12 GB. No GPU is needed. On a ~4 GB CPU/iGPU kiosk this is disproportionate; the sensible placement is a build-time/CI conformance gate or a clinic-side/HIS server, with only the emitted JSON on the kiosk.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: No model accuracy/F1/ROUGE metrics apply; quality is conformance correctness. Matchbox reuses the exact official HL7 reference validator, so its validation semantics match the standard toolchain, and it is trusted enough to be wired into the IHE Gazelle EVS Client used at Connectathons (a de facto interoperability correctness signal). A worked example in the docs shows a Patient validation completing in 0.015s. Matchbox also added a validation-statistics feature (v4.1.6) and custom metrics for tracking validation behaviour.
performance_metrics.latency: No official benchmark. The validation tutorial reports Duration: 0.015s for a simple Patient profile validation. A practical caveat is first-call cost: creating an engine for an IG 'might have duration of half a minute', which is why igsPreloaded exists to cache engines in memory at the cost of RAM. This warm-up trade-off is the main latency consideration for a kiosk-side or CI validator.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Pure Java, no GPU. JDK 11+ for the engine (JRE 17 re-added in 4.1.6), JDK 17/21 for the server. Docs recommend at least 2.5 GB RAM for the container depending on the number of IGs, and the Docker image heap requirement was raised to 12 GB in v4.1.3. A PostgreSQL database is typical for persistent IG storage, plus the JVM. The engine CLI fat jar is over 100 MB. This is heavier than a 4 GB kiosk should host alongside the kiosk application.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Modest open-source adoption but high institutional trust: GitHub at verification shows 37 stars, 29 forks, 5 watchers, 2,001 commits, 9 open issues and 1 open pull request; 115+ tagged releases. Supply-chain maturity signals include Qodana, Trivy image scans, SBOM tooling and Dependabot. Real-world scale is qualitative: production use validating messages with no internet call-outs, and Connectathon/Gazelle EVS Client integration plus the Swiss community. The public test server is open for trials.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Correctness is established by conformance testing, not clinical or ML evaluation: per-release integration and unit test suites that re-verify pinned core versions and patched files, a JMeter load-testing example, security scanners (Qodana, Trivy), and CI workflows that publish Docker (Google Artifact Registry) and Maven Central artifacts. Cross-checking is implicit through reuse of the official HL7 validator and Connectathon participation. For Module C the meaningful verification would be loading ndhm.in and confirming expected OperationOutcome on known-good and known-bad OPConsultRecord bundles.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: Matchbox is the strongest candidate for an offline NRCeS-conformance gate for Module C's emitted OPConsultRecord/DocumentBundle, and in several respects it fits MediKiosk's constraints better than the HAPI JPA starter alone. Three reasons: (1) it exists specifically to run IG validation with no internet, with packages loaded from classpath/filesystem and an internal terminology server - exactly the offline-first, India-residency posture Module C needs; (2) its validating engine is the same official HL7 org.hl7.fhir.core validator HAPI uses, so results are interoperable with the Indian ABDM validation pipeline that expects the HL7 validator; and (3) it adds mapping/transformation via the FHIR Mapping Language, which is directly useful if Module C ever needs to map legacy HIS data or CDA/discharge documents into ABDM-shaped resources. It supplies no elicitation, summarisation, document OCR or AYUSH clinical logic - it is purely the conformance/transform substrate beneath Module C.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) Matchbox (engine or server) as the offline NRCeS/profile conformance gate in Module C's build/CI and any clinic-side validation, configured with the ndhm.in IG vendored locally; (2) the preload-from-classpath/filesystem pattern plus internal terminology server to eliminate runtime internet dependence; (3) the httpReadOnly deployment posture so a locked-down validator cannot have IGs mutated over the API; (4) the OperationOutcome-with-loaded-packages-and-parameters enrichment, which gives a legible, auditable conformance record for physician attestation; (5) the FHIR Mapping Language + StructureMap/$transform capability as an optional data-normalisation path. Reject or adapt: (1) running the full Matchbox Spring Boot server on the ~4 GB kiosk - the 2.5-12 GB heap guidance rules it out, so use it build-time or clinic-side; (2) assuming Matchbox validates AYUSH/NAMASTE terminology - it will not, because NAMASTE is not bound into the ABDM IG, so AYUSH coding needs a separate layer; (3) relying on the internal terminology server for SNOMED CT/LOINC/display checks - it is deliberately limited and will skip intensional ValueSet expansion; (4) the optional LLM/AI error-analysis and MCP features - unnecessary, network/LLM-dependent surface for a deterministic kiosk pipeline; (5) treating 'validates against base R4' as sufficient - the ndhm.in package must be loaded for the result to be ABDM-relevant.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: The decisive open risk is the unproven NDHM/ABDM path: no public Matchbox configuration, deployment example or issue loading ndhm.in was found, and Matchbox's own test/preload configs are Swiss-focused, so ABDM profile validation through Matchbox must be proven locally before it is relied on. Practical frictions that are documented in Matchbox's own history include package loading fragility (custom SearchParameter startup exceptions, unversioned canonical resolution bugs, IGs failing to resolve when mistaken for core packages, memory leaks with precached IGs), engine warm-up latency (up to ~30s per IG on first use), and a resource profile that is heavy for constrained hardware (2.5 GB recommended, 12 GB Docker heap default). It is JVM enterprise infrastructure with a JDK floor and PostgreSQL dependency for persistence, so it does not belong on a 4 GB kiosk. Terminology completeness is a false-confidence risk offline: the internal tx server does not validate display names and cannot expand intensional ValueSets. The project is single-vendor (ahdis) and release numbering is fast-moving, so pinning a version and vendoring packages is essential. Finally, its AI/LLM analysis features introduce optional network and third-party model dependencies that a kiosk deployment should disable.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: Matchbox is infrastructure, not a competitor, and it reinforces rather than erodes MediKiosk's differentiators: it is the open, self-hostable, offline-capable, standards-faithful validation layer that makes 'NRCeS-conformant emission' testable and keeps validation on Indian soil. It does nothing on the axes where MediKiosk differentiates - no elicitation, no bilingual summary generation, no document digitisation, no AYUSH/Prakriti handling, no per-field provenance, no physician attestation. Compared with HAPI alone, Matchbox's edge is explicit offline IG preloading, an internal terminology server, and mapping - but it makes no difference to the moat: any ABDM entrant can adopt it, so standards conformance remains table stakes and MediKiosk's defensibility must stay in the elicitation-to-structured-summary layer and the AYUSH gap.

business_info.license: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0), stated on matchbox.health and present as the repository LICENSE. Permissive, commercial-use friendly. Underlying components (HAPI FHIR, org.hl7.fhir.core) are also open source; bundled terminology/LOINC content carries its own notices.
business_info.pricing: The software is free and open source; ahdis offers commercial support and services separately via ahdis.ch. No paid tier is required to use Matchbox. Hosting the public test server is a free courtesy.
business_info.funding: [uncertain] No external funding round, grant or investor is disclosed. Matchbox is developed and funded as part of ahdis ag's commercial interoperability consulting/engineering business (open-core-style: free Apache-2.0 tooling plus paid support). Detailed corporate financials were not researched.
business_info.commercial_status: Open-source project with a commercial-support business model, maintained by a for-profit consultancy (ahdis ag). Free to use; production support is a paid ahdis service.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Direct alternatives in the FHIR validation niche: the plain HL7 org.hl7.fhir.core validator_cli.jar (the same engine Matchbox wraps, no server/preload management), HAPI FHIR's own validator/JPA server, Firely .NET SDK / Vonk / Firely Server (Netherlands), the web-based HL7 FHIR Validator, and cloud FHIR validators (Microsoft/AWS/GCP). In the ABDM-specific space the practical 'validation layer' is the HL7 validator CLI with the ndhm.in package (as shown in Indian example repos), which Matchbox can replace with an offline server/library. Matchbox's distinctive position versus all of these is offline IG preloading plus an internal terminology server plus mapping.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: IHE Gazelle EVS Client (validation API, used at Connectathons), an internal terminology server endpoint, external terminology servers (tx.fhir.org, Ontoserver), FHIR package servers and direct package URLs/classpath/filesystem loading, SDC Questionnaire/$extract, FML/StructureMap transforms, CDA-to-FHIR mapping, and MCP server integration with optional LLM error analysis. It integrates with any FHIR R4/R4B/R5 endpoint. No ABDM gateway (HIP/HIU/PHR) or Indian Health Locker integration is provided or claimed; loading NRCeS ndhm.in would be a user configuration, not a built-in integration.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: Matchbox sits in the same trustworthy open FHIR-tooling ecosystem as HAPI and the HL7 validator, so adopting it is low-risk and well-precedented, and its Connectathon/Gazelle role adds credibility for a government-facing conformance story. For MediKiosk the ecosystem implication is that offline NRCeS validation is achievable with free, self-hostable tooling - India residency and offline-first need not be traded away for conformance. The main ecosystem risk is that the ABDM/NRCeS package distribution is not fully reliable (NRCeS example repos warn the package.tgz URL may change), so a Matchbox-based pipeline must vendor the ndhm.in package rather than fetch it live. A secondary consideration is single-vendor maintenance (ahdis), mitigated by the permissive license and by the fact that Matchbox tracks upstream HAPI/core continuously.

history.release_date: Early 2021 - Matchbox began as an ahdis extension of the hapifhir/hapi-fhir-jpaserver-starter for FHIR validation and FHIR Mapping Language transformation; the changelog records a 3.x line through 2022-2023 and the project has been continuously released since. [uncertain] The exact first tagged/public release date was not retrieved.
history.key_milestones: 2023: 3.x line matured with validation GUI, suppress warn/info, an HTTP read-only mode and a simple internal terminology server for offline validation (3.5.0, Dec 2023); 3.7.0 (Mar 2024) added R5 support and the new Gazelle validation API; 3.8.1 (Apr 2024) moved to JDK 21; 3.9.0 (Sep 2024) added R4B and cross-version FML transforms. 2025: 4.0.0 (Mar 2025) upgraded to HAPI 8.0.0 and core 6.5.15; 4.0.13-4.0.14 (Oct 2025) added MCP server integration; 4.0.16 (Jan 2026) removed auto-install of IGs and pinned THO. 2026: 4.1.0 (Mar 2026) upgraded to HAPI 8.8.0 and Spring Boot 3.5.12; 4.1.6 (May 2026) re-added JRE 17 support and introduced validation statistics; 4.1.12 (Aug 2026) updated core to 6.10.0, added SSRF protection and raised max request size to 100 MB; 4.1.14 (Aug 2026) added Bundle/$get-profiles and document-Bundle profile inference.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: The window from ~March to September 2026 shows one of the fastest release cadences in the FHIR tooling space. v4.1.0 (2026-03-30) and 4.1.1/4.1.2/4.1.3 (late March/early April) upgraded HAPI FHIR to 8.8.0 and Spring Boot 3.5.12, fixed a $validate-code ClassCastException, integrated new xver packages, added a Docker HEALTHCHECK, and raised the container heap requirement to 12 GB. v4.1.4-4.1.7 (April-May) were mostly CVE/dependency hardening plus a FHIRPath test for data-absent-reason. v4.1.8 (2026-05-26) fixed custom SearchParameter loading and updated core to 6.9.8. v4.1.9 (2026-05-27) fixed an Undertow multipart DoS (CVE-2026-3260). v4.1.10-4.1.11 (June-July) reworked MCP validation to return an OperationOutcome plus a prompt and upgraded Angular 22. v4.1.12 (2026-08-11) moved to core 6.10.0 and HAPI 8.10.1, added SSRF protection, and fixed the Ambiguous type id bug when another FHIR version is declared as an IG dependency. v4.1.13 (2026-08-14) forced Spring dependency versions to close several CVEs. v4.1.14 (2026-08-31) added Bundle/$get-profiles to infer validation profiles from a document Bundle's Composition type/category, added validation-statistics DB columns, and made StructureMap/$transform always available. v4.1.15 (2026-09-11) updated to HAPI FHIR 8.12.0 and core 6.10.4 and fixed unversioned-canonical resolution. v4.1.16 (2026-09-14) fixed MCP server startup and the $get-profiles response type. Nothing in this window regresses offline validation; the document-Bundle profile inference and $get-profiles additions are directly useful to an ABDM document-Bundle workflow.

market_positioning.target_users: Health-IT engineers and integrators building FHIR implementations; national/regional e-health programmes and IG authors (especially Swiss CH EPR and IHE profiles); vendors and test labs that need an offline, API-callable validator; and HL7 Connectathon participants via the Gazelle tooling. Developer/integrator infrastructure, not an end-user product.
market_positioning.market_segment: FHIR tooling - validation and mapping middleware/server engines; the conformance layer beneath national health-data-exchange programmes and EHR products. Not intake, ambient scribing, PHR, AYUSH software, diagnostics kiosk or benchmarking.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: Matchbox presents itself as 'an open source initiative to support testing and implementation of FHIR-based solutions and to map or capture health data into HL7 FHIR', with the pitch that it can be 'deployed as a microservice in your IT infrastructure', that 'implementation guides can be preloaded ... without requiring access to the internet or external package servers at runtime', and that it is 'used in production for validating messages ensuring that no call outs to the internet are made'. It is 'licensed under the business-friendly Apache Software License 2.0' and is 'based on the HAPI FHIR project', with a public test server offered for evaluation.
